title: Resource Hierarchy and Azure Resource Manager (Basic)
reading:
Today's menu

By the end of this lunch you will be able to:

- Explain the levels of the Azure resource hierarchy, from the Microsoft Entra tenant down to a single resource, and what each level is for.
- Describe how Azure Resource Manager handles every management request, and tell control-plane operations from data-plane operations.
- Read a resource ID and predict which roles, policies, locks, budgets and tags apply to a resource through its scope.
- Organise resources with resource groups, naming conventions, tags and locks, and find them again with Azure Resource Graph.

Meanwhile at Nusantara Retail

Three weeks of experiments have left their mark. The lab subscription now holds a resource group called test, two more called rg1 and rg-new, a virtual machine named server-baru-final2 and a storage account called dewitest123. Nobody remembers which of them belong to the storefront.

Requests are piling up on your desk. The finance team wants to see what the storefront costs, separately from the new stock-sync project. Rizky, the contractor, needs to manage the storefront and nothing else. Pak Budi wants a guarantee that nobody, not even an administrator in a hurry, can delete the storage account that will hold every product photo. And Ibu Sari wants rules such as "customer data stays in Jakarta" to be set once and enforced everywhere.

None of these requests is about a particular service. They are all about structure. Today's question: how should Nusantara Retail organise its Azure estate so that access, rules and costs follow the structure automatically?

Reading

1. Six levels, from tenant to resource

Every Azure resource sits at the bottom of a hierarchy, and each level above it is a place where you can attach rules that flow down. Read it from the top:

- The Microsoft Entra tenant is the organisation's identity directory: users, groups and applications. Every subscription trusts exactly one tenant. Signing in happens here; Lunch 05 covers it in depth.
- The root management group sits directly under the tenant. Each tenant has exactly one, shown in the portal as Tenant root group, and its ID is the tenant ID. Every management group and subscription folds up to it, new subscriptions land in it by default, and it can't be moved or deleted. Nobody has access to it by default: a Global Administrator must first elevate their own access.
- Management groups are containers for subscriptions and for other management groups. A tree can be up to six levels deep below the root (the root and the subscription level don't count), a tenant can hold up to 10,000 management groups, and every management group or subscription has exactly one parent.
- Subscriptions hold resource groups and are the unit of billing and scale (more on that below).
- Resource groups are containers for resources that share a lifecycle.
- Resources are the things you actually use and pay for: virtual machines, storage accounts, web apps, databases.

Level | Main purpose | Rules worth remembering | Nusantara Retail example
Microsoft Entra tenant | Identities and sign-in | Each subscription trusts exactly one tenant | The company directory
Root management group | Top of the governance tree | ID equals the tenant ID; can't be moved or deleted; no access by default | Tenant root group
Management groups | Group subscriptions to apply rules at scale | Up to six levels below the root; one parent each | mg-nusa, mg-nusa-prod, mg-nusa-nonprod
Subscriptions | Billing, quota and access boundary | One parent management group; trusts one tenant | sub-nusa-prod, sub-nusa-dev
Resource groups | Lifecycle container | Each resource in exactly one group; no nesting | rg-storefront-prod, rg-shared-prod
Resources | The services you use | Type comes from a resource provider; most names are permanent | app-nusa-shop, stnusaimg01

Subscriptions deserve a closer look, because they are three boundaries at once. They are a billing boundary: usage is collected per subscription and rolls up to the billing account above it, so separate subscriptions give you clean cost separation without any tagging discipline. They are a scale boundary: quotas and limits, such as how many vCPUs you may run in a region, apply per subscription, so an experiment in development can't eat production's quota. And they are a natural access and policy boundary. That is why the most common first step is simply two subscriptions, one for production and one for everything else.

Important: Management groups are tenant-wide. The first time anyone uses them, Azure creates the root management group and places every existing subscription under it, and unless an administrator has turned on hierarchy protection, any user in the tenant can create management groups. Practise only in your own lab tenant, never in a company tenant, and never move a work subscription around to "see what happens".

2. Azure Resource Manager: one front door for every tool

In Lunch 01 you saw that the portal, the Azure CLI, Azure PowerShell and every SDK send their requests to Azure Resource Manager (ARM). It's worth knowing what ARM does with each request, because every rule in this lunch is enforced there. ARM authenticates the caller with a Microsoft Entra token, checks Azure RBAC role assignments at the target scope and every scope above it, evaluates Azure Policy, checks resource locks, records the operation in the activity log, and only then hands the request to the right resource provider. Because every tool goes through the same API, they all get the same answers: the portal has no secret powers that the CLI lacks.

A resource provider is the service behind a family of resource types, named by a namespace such as Microsoft.Compute, Microsoft.Network, Microsoft.Storage or Microsoft.Web. Each provider offers resource types, so the full type of a storage account is Microsoft.Storage/storageAccounts. Some types are children of others: a blob container is Microsoft.Storage/storageAccounts/blobServices/containers. Each type also publishes its API versions (dated, such as 2024-01-01) and the regions where it's available, which is exactly what you queried in Lab 03.

Everything ARM handles is the control plane: creating, configuring and deleting resources through https://management.azure.com. Using a resource is the data plane: reading a blob from https://stnusaimg01.blob.core.windows.net, querying a database, or connecting to a VM over SSH. Data-plane requests go straight to the service's own endpoint and are governed by that service's own authorization: Microsoft Entra data roles, access keys, shared access signatures or database logins. Two consequences follow. The data plane keeps working even if the control plane is briefly unavailable, so your shop stays open. And rules enforced by ARM, such as locks, don't automatically protect what happens on the data plane.

Because every control-plane write passes through ARM, the activity log becomes a reliable record of who created, changed or deleted what, and when, at every scope. When someone asks "who deleted the test VM on Friday?", that is where you look (Lunch 16).

ARM also understands desired state. When you send it a template that describes resources, it works out what to create and what already exists, so deploying the same file twice gives the same result. That idea powers infrastructure as code with Bicep in Lunch 20.

3. Scopes, inheritance and resource IDs

A scope is the place where you attach a setting: a management group, a subscription, a resource group or a single resource. The rule that makes the hierarchy useful is inheritance: settings flow down to everything below, including things created later. Assign the finance team a reader role on mg-nusa-prod and they can read every subscription, resource group and resource beneath it, even next year's. Put a lock on rg-shared-prod and every resource added to that group later is protected too. But not everything flows down:

Setting | Can be attached at | Flows down? | Watch out for
Azure RBAC role assignment | Management group, subscription, resource group, resource | Yes | Permissions from all scopes add up; assign as low as practical (Lunch 05)
Azure Policy assignment | Management group, subscription, resource group | Yes, with exemptions possible | Denials happen at ARM, before anything is built (Lunch 18)
Resource lock | Subscription, resource group, resource (not management groups) | Yes; the most restrictive lock wins | Blocks everyone, Owners included
Budget | Management group (not for every agreement type), subscription, resource group | Covers the cost of everything inside | Sends alerts; it doesn't stop spending (Lunch 19)
Tag | Subscription, resource group, resource (not management groups) | No | Copy or enforce tags with Azure Policy

Every scope, and every resource, has an address called a resource ID. It is the path from the subscription down to the resource, and it's what scripts, templates, role assignments, locks and alerts use to point at things:

/subscriptions/8f2a…41c7/resourceGroups/rg-shared-prod/providers/Microsoft.Storage/storageAccounts/stnusaimg01

Segment | Example | What it tells you
/subscriptions/{id} | /subscriptions/8f2a…41c7 | Which subscription, and therefore which tenant and bill
/resourceGroups/{name} | /resourceGroups/rg-shared-prod | Which resource group: the lifecycle and a scope
/providers/{namespace} | /providers/Microsoft.Storage | Which resource provider serves it
/{type} | /storageAccounts | The resource type within that provider
/{name} | /stnusaimg01 | The resource name

The higher scopes use the same pattern. A subscription is /subscriptions/{id}, a resource group is /subscriptions/{id}/resourceGroups/{name}, and a management group is /providers/Microsoft.Management/managementGroups/{id}. Child resources add more type-and-name pairs to their parent's ID, for example …/storageAccounts/stnusaimg01/blobServices/default/containers/images. Locks and role assignments are extension resources that hang off another ID: a lock on that account lives at …/stnusaimg01/providers/Microsoft.Authorization/locks/{lock name}. The segment names are case-insensitive, so you will see both resourceGroups and resourcegroups in real output; compare IDs without caring about case.

4. Resource groups, moves, names and tags

A resource group should hold resources that share a lifecycle: you deploy, update and delete them together. A few rules follow from that design:

- Each resource lives in exactly one resource group. Resource groups can't be nested, and they can't be renamed.
- A resource group has a location, which is where Azure stores its metadata. Its resources may live in other regions, but keeping them in the same region is simpler; if the group's region is unavailable, Resource Manager reroutes control-plane requests to a backup region.
- Deleting a resource group deletes everything inside it. That is the cleanup superpower the labs rely on, and exactly why production groups deserve a lock.
- A resource can still talk to resources in other groups. The storefront in rg-storefront-prod reads photos from the storage account in rg-shared-prod, because the two have different owners and lifecycles.

A common beginner mistake is to group by resource type: all VMs in rg-vms, all databases in rg-databases. It looks tidy until you need to delete one application, give one team access to its own pieces, or see what one workload costs. Group by workload and environment instead, plus a group for genuinely shared services, and let the resource names and tags tell you what each item is.

Moving a resource between resource groups or subscriptions (within the same tenant) is possible for many resource types, and it changes less than you might fear. The resource stays in its region and keeps running; only its resource group or subscription, and therefore its resource ID, changes, so update any script, dashboard or alert that uses the old ID. While the move runs, both resource groups are locked against creates, updates and deletes: usually for minutes, at most four hours. Not every type can move (NAT gateways and AKS clusters are examples at the time of writing), child resources always travel with their parent, and Azure validates the request first. Role assignments made directly on the moved resource don't come along, while the resource's own tags do. A read-only lock on either resource group blocks the move entirely.

Names deserve a plan, because most of them can't be changed after creation. The Cloud Adoption Framework (CAF) suggests building names from a few components: a short abbreviation of the resource type, the workload, the environment, sometimes the region, and an instance number. That gives names such as rg-storefront-prod, vm-web-prod-001 and vnet-shared-idc-001. Common abbreviations are rg, vm, vnet, snet, nsg, pip, st (storage account), kv (key vault) and mg (management group). Some names must be unique across all of Azure because they become DNS names: a storage account name, for instance, is 3 to 24 lowercase letters and digits, without hyphens. Keep anything that might change, such as the owner or the cost centre, out of names and put it in tags.

Tags are name-value labels on resources, resource groups and subscriptions (but not on management groups), up to 50 per item. They drive cost reports, automation and searches. Tag names are case-insensitive, but values are case-sensitive, so ecommerce and Ecommerce show up as two different cost centres. Tags are stored as plain text and appear in cost exports and logs, so never put secrets or personal data in them. And the rule that surprises everyone: tags are not inherited. A tag on a resource group does not appear on the resources inside it. If every resource must carry the group's cost centre, use Azure Policy to copy or enforce it (Lunch 18).

Tip: Agree on a short list of mandatory tags, such as costCenter, env, owner and app, with fixed spellings and allowed values, before the first production deployment. Retagging hundreds of resources later is slow and error-prone, and the cost reports for the months in between stay messy forever.

5. Locks and Azure Resource Graph

A resource lock protects resources from accidents, regardless of who is signed in. There are two kinds:

Lock (CLI name) | Portal name | Blocks | Still allowed
CanNotDelete | Delete | Deleting the locked resource, or anything under a locked scope | Reading and changing settings
ReadOnly | Read-only | Deleting and every change, including some actions that feel like reads | Reading (GET requests)

Locks can be set on a subscription, a resource group or a resource, and they are inherited by everything below; when locks at several levels apply, the most restrictive one wins. A lock overrides permissions, so even an Owner has to remove the lock before deleting. Only roles that include the Microsoft.Authorization/locks/* actions, such as Owner and User Access Administrator, can create or remove locks; a Contributor can't. And a CanNotDelete lock on a single resource stops its whole resource group from being deleted: Azure doesn't do partial deletes.

The ReadOnly surprise. ARM enforces locks on the control plane by looking at the type of request. Reads (GET) pass. Creates, updates and deletes are blocked, and so are POST actions, because ARM can't know whether a POST changes something. Many operations that feel like reads are POST actions: listing a storage account's access keys is a POST, deliberately, because the keys give full access to the data and shouldn't come back from an ordinary read. Starting or restarting a VM, scaling an App Service plan and moving resources in or out of a locked group are blocked too. A ReadOnly lock on a production resource group can therefore break deployments, automation and even an application that fetches its storage keys at startup. Use CanNotDelete for "don't delete this" and role assignments for "don't change this".

Warning: Locks protect resources, not the data inside them. A CanNotDelete or ReadOnly lock on a storage account doesn't stop someone with data access from deleting blobs through the data plane. Protect data with least-privilege data roles, soft delete, versioning and immutability (Lunch 24).

Azure Resource Graph answers the question "what do we have, and where?" across every subscription and management group you can read, in seconds. You query it with a subset of the Kusto Query Language (KQL). The Resources table holds resources, and ResourceContainers holds subscriptions, resource groups and management groups:

Resources
| where tags.costCenter == 'ecommerce'
| project name, type, resourceGroup, location

You can run queries in the portal's Resource Graph Explorer, with az graph query in the Azure CLI (its extension installs itself the first time) or from PowerShell. Resource Graph is read-only, it only shows what your roles allow you to see, and it returns up to 1,000 records per query by default, with paging for more.

6. How it fits together for Nusantara Retail

You can now turn the pile of requests into a structure. Under the Tenant root group, create mg-nusa for the company and two children, mg-nusa-prod and mg-nusa-nonprod. Production runs in sub-nusa-prod; development, testing and Rizky's work run in sub-nusa-dev. Inside production, the web app lives in rg-storefront-prod and the product-photo storage account in rg-shared-prod, because other apps, such as the stores' tablets, will use it too.

Then the rules attach themselves to the right scopes. The finance team gets a reader role on mg-nusa-prod. An Azure Policy assignment there allows only Indonesia Central, which you chose in Lunch 03. A CanNotDelete lock on rg-shared-prod answers Pak Budi. Rizky gets a contributor role on rg-storefront-dev and nothing else (Lunch 05). Every resource carries costCenter, env, owner and app tags, a budget watches each subscription (Lunch 19), and a saved Resource Graph query lists anything that is missing a costCenter tag. In the lab you will build a small slice of this design yourself.

Pause and think: next year Dewi creates a new subscription for a loyalty-card app. Will the finance team's reader role and the location policy on mg-nusa-prod apply to it automatically? What has to happen first?

Going deeper: Lunch 31 · Resource Hierarchy and Governance (Advanced) designs a full landing-zone management group hierarchy and applies governance at scale.

Field notes from Stefanus

The delete test. For every resource group in a design, I ask one question: if I delete this group tonight, should everything inside it disappear too? If the answer is "yes, except the database" or "yes, but not the photos", the exception belongs in another group. That single question catches most lifecycle mistakes while they are still cheap to fix, before scripts, dashboards and alerts depend on the names and resource IDs. My second habit: when an error message contains a resource ID, I read it left to right like a postal address and check each scope on the way down, because the lock or policy that blocks you is often inherited from a level you weren't looking at. And names carry only what never changes; owners, cost centres and project codes change, so they go in tags.

Go further

- What is Azure Resource Manager? (https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/azure-resource-manager/management/overview) — scopes, resource groups, resource group locations and how Resource Manager stays resilient.
- What are Azure management groups? (https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/governance/management-groups/overview) — the root management group, the limits and the permissions needed to build and change the hierarchy.
- Lock your Azure resources to protect your infrastructure (https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/azure-resource-manager/management/lock-resources) — the full list of operations that locks block, including the ReadOnly surprises.
- Define your naming convention (https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/cloud-adoption-framework/ready/azure-best-practices/resource-naming) — the Cloud Adoption Framework's naming components, with links to the abbreviation list.

quiz.q: The finance team must be able to read every production resource, including subscriptions that will be added to production later. Where do you assign their role?
quiz.a: On the mg-nusa-prod management group. Why: role assignments are inherited by every subscription, resource group and resource below the scope, including ones created or moved there later.

quiz.q: Pak Budi puts a ReadOnly lock on rg-shared-prod. The next morning the storefront can't fetch the storage account keys and an operator can't restart a VM in that group. What happened?
quiz.a: Both operations are POST actions, and a ReadOnly lock blocks every control-plane request except reads. Why: ARM can't tell whether a POST changes something, so it blocks them all; a CanNotDelete lock would have protected the group without breaking them.

quiz.q: Dewi tags rg-storefront-prod with costCenter=ecommerce, but the cost report grouped by costCenter shows nothing for the web app inside it. Why?
quiz.a: Tags are not inherited: the web app itself has no costCenter tag. Why: tags stay on the item you put them on; tag the resources directly or use Azure Policy to copy the tag from the resource group.

quiz.q: A script saves the storage account's resource ID. After you move the account from rg-storefront-prod to rg-shared-prod, the script fails with "resource not found". The account still works for customers. Explain.
quiz.a: The resource ID contains the resource group name, so the move gave the account a new ID; the region, data and endpoints didn't change. Why: a move only changes the resource group or subscription segment of the ID, so update everything that refers to the old one.

quiz.q: With a CanNotDelete lock on the storage account, can a user who holds a data role still delete blobs inside it?
quiz.a: Yes. Why: locks apply to control-plane operations through Azure Resource Manager; deleting a blob is a data-plane operation, so protect data with least-privilege data roles, soft delete and versioning.

takeaways: The hierarchy runs tenant → root management group → management groups (up to six levels) → subscriptions → resource groups → resources, and every item has exactly one parent.

Azure Resource Manager is the single front door for management: it authenticates, applies RBAC, Policy and locks, logs the request and calls the resource provider. Using a resource happens on the separate data plane.
Roles, policies and locks flow down from the scope where you set them, and a budget covers everything below its scope; tags don't inherit.
A resource ID spells out subscription, resource group, provider, type and name, so moving a resource changes its ID but never its region.
Keep order with CAF-style names, a short list of mandatory tags, the right lock (beware ReadOnly) and Azure Resource Graph queries.

lab.title: Organise Nusantara Retail
lab.text:
What you'll build

Nusantara Retail is replacing its pile of experiments with a structure. You create two tagged resource groups, one for the storefront and one for shared services, and a storage account for product photos. You take the account's resource ID apart, prove that resource group tags don't reach the resources inside, and watch two kinds of lock stop you: a CanNotDelete lock blocks a deletion, and a ReadOnly lock blocks something that looks like a simple read. Then you move the account to the shared resource group, where it belongs, and find everything again with Azure Resource Graph. Optionally, you create a management group in your own tenant.

Before you start

- An Azure subscription where you are Owner (see Lab 01 (https://stefpin.github.io/azure-fundamentals-lunches/en/labs/01-before-you-begin.html)). Creating and removing locks needs Owner or User Access Administrator; Contributor isn't enough.
- Azure Cloud Shell (Bash) — open shell.azure.com. Nothing to install.
- Get the lab files and load the shared settings:

git clone https://github.com/stefpin/azure-fundamentals-lunches.git   # first time only
cd azure-fundamentals-lunches/labs/04-resource-hierarchy-basic
source ../common/config.sh
RG_SHOP=$(rg_name 04 shop)
RG_SHARED=$(rg_name 04 shared)
ST="stnusaimg${SUFFIX}"
ST_TYPE="Microsoft.Storage/storageAccounts"

- This lab has no setup.sh: you create everything yourself.
- If Cloud Shell times out and restarts, cd back into the lab folder and run the five lines after cd again. Task 3 shows how to get the storage account's ID back into ST_ID.

Important: Lab resources cost money while they exist (an empty storage account costs next to nothing, but clean up anyway). If you stop halfway, run Clean up: it removes any lock you left behind before deleting the resource groups.

Choose your mode

Mode | For you if… | How
Guided | you want every step explained | follow Tasks 1–8 below
Challenge | you already know the basics | read only the Challenge brief, build it your way, then run bash verify.sh

Task 1 · Two tagged resource groups

The storefront and the shared services have different owners and lifecycles, so they get separate resource groups. ensure_rg creates each group with the course's course and lunch tags (the cleanup script finds groups by them); then you merge in your own tags.

ensure_rg "$RG_SHOP" 04
ensure_rg "$RG_SHARED" 04

az tag update --resource-id "$(az group show --name "$RG_SHOP" --query id --output tsv)" \
  --operation Merge --tags project=storefront env=lab costCenter=ecommerce --output none
az tag update --resource-id "$(az group show --name "$RG_SHARED" --query id --output tsv)" \
  --operation Merge --tags project=shared-services env=lab costCenter=it --output none

az group list --query "[?tags.lunch=='04'].{name:name, location:location, project:tags.project, costCenter:tags.costCenter}" \
  --output table

Merge adds tags and updates existing ones. Replace would throw away every tag that isn't in your list, including the course and lunch tags that cleanup relies on, so be careful which one you pick.

Tip: Prefer the portal? Resource groups › rg-lunch04-shop-… › Tags: add the three tags and select Apply. The portal edits the same tag set that the CLI does.

Checkpoint: the table shows both groups in your LOCATION, with storefront/ecommerce and shared-services/it.

Task 2 · A storage account, and tags that don't flow down

Create the product-photo storage account in the storefront's resource group, then look at its tags.

az storage account create --name "$ST" --resource-group "$RG_SHOP" --location "$LOCATION" \
  --sku Standard_LRS --kind StorageV2 --min-tls-version TLS1_2 --allow-blob-public-access false \
  --output none

az storage account show --name "$ST" --resource-group "$RG_SHOP" --query tags

The answer is {} (or nothing at all): the group's project, env and costCenter tags did not flow down to the account. Tag the resource itself:

ST_ID=$(az storage account show --name "$ST" --resource-group "$RG_SHOP" --query id --output tsv)
az tag update --resource-id "$ST_ID" --operation Merge --tags app=product-images env=lab --output none
az tag list --resource-id "$ST_ID" --query properties.tags

Checkpoint: the account exists in the shop group and carries exactly the tags you gave it, app and env, and none of the group's tags.

Task 3 · Take the resource ID apart

A resource ID is the address Azure Resource Manager uses for everything. Print it, then split it on the slashes.

echo "$ST_ID"
IFS='/' read -r -a parts <<< "$ST_ID"
for i in "${!parts[@]}"; do printf '%2d  %s\n' "$i" "${parts[$i]}"; done

Read the numbered output: 1–2 are the subscription (keep the ID to yourself), 3–4 the resource group, 5–6 the resource provider namespace, 7 the resource type and 8 the name. The ID alone is enough to find the resource:

az resource show --ids "$ST_ID" --query "{name:name, type:type, location:location, group:resourceGroup}" --output table

Now look at the resource provider behind it, the resource types it offers and the newest API versions of the storage account type:

az provider show --namespace Microsoft.Storage --query "{namespace:namespace, state:registrationState}" --output table
az provider show --namespace Microsoft.Storage --query "resourceTypes[].resourceType" --output tsv | head -n 12
az provider show --namespace Microsoft.Storage \
  --query "resourceTypes[?resourceType=='storageAccounts'].apiVersions | [0][:3]" --output tsv

Tip: Lost ST_ID after a Cloud Shell restart? Get it back with ST_ID=$(az storage account list --query "[?name=='${ST}'].id | [0]" --output tsv), which finds the account in whichever resource group it is in now.

Checkpoint: you can say which part of the ID is the subscription, the resource group, the provider namespace (Microsoft.Storage), the type (storageAccounts) and the name. The provider shows Registered.

Task 4 · A CanNotDelete lock blocks deletion

Pak Budi wants the photo store protected against accidental deletion. A CanNotDelete lock (called Delete in the portal) does that for everyone, Owners included.

az lock create --name lock-nodelete --lock-type CanNotDelete \
  --resource-group "$RG_SHOP" --resource "$ST" --resource-type "$ST_TYPE" \
  --notes "Product photos - do not delete" --output none

az lock list --resource-group "$RG_SHOP" --resource "$ST" --resource-type "$ST_TYPE" \
  --query "[].{name:name, level:level}" --output table

Give the lock a few seconds, then try to delete the account. The az lock show … && part is a safety net: the delete only runs if the lock really exists.

sleep 15
az lock show --name lock-nodelete --resource-group "$RG_SHOP" \
  --resource "$ST" --resource-type "$ST_TYPE" --output none \
  && az storage account delete --name "$ST" --resource-group "$RG_SHOP" --yes

The delete fails with an error code ScopeLocked and a message saying that the scope can't perform the delete operation because a scope is locked. Changes are still allowed, because this lock only blocks deletion:

az tag update --resource-id "$ST_ID" --operation Merge --tags owner=dewi --output none \
  && echo "Tag added: a CanNotDelete lock still allows changes."

Remove the lock before the next task:

az lock delete --name lock-nodelete --resource-group "$RG_SHOP" --resource "$ST" --resource-type "$ST_TYPE"

Tip: Prefer the portal? Storage account › Settings › Locks › Add, lock type Delete. Then try Delete on the account's Overview page and read the notification.

Checkpoint: the delete was refused with ScopeLocked, the tag update worked, and the lock list is empty again.

Task 5 · A ReadOnly lock blocks more than you expect

A ReadOnly lock (Read-only in the portal) lets everyone read and nobody change anything. "Reading" means GET requests only, and that's where the surprise comes from.

az lock create --name lock-readonly --lock-type ReadOnly \
  --resource-group "$RG_SHOP" --resource "$ST" --resource-type "$ST_TYPE" --output none
sleep 15

# 1) Reading the account's properties is a GET: allowed
az storage account show --name "$ST" --resource-group "$RG_SHOP" --query "{name:name, sku:sku.name}" --output table

# 2) Listing the access keys is a POST: blocked (the query prints only how many keys, never the keys themselves)
az storage account keys list --account-name "$ST" --resource-group "$RG_SHOP" --query "length(@)" --output tsv

# 3) Changing a tag is a write: blocked
az tag update --resource-id "$ST_ID" --operation Merge --tags reviewed=yes --output none

Commands 2 and 3 fail with ScopeLocked. Listing keys feels like a read, but it's a POST action on purpose: the keys give full access to every blob in the account, so Azure doesn't hand them out through an ordinary GET. A ReadOnly lock blocks every POST, because Resource Manager can't know which POST actions change something. An application that fetches its storage keys at startup would break the moment someone adds this lock.

Remove the lock and confirm that keys can be listed again (still only the count):

az lock delete --name lock-readonly --resource-group "$RG_SHOP" --resource "$ST" --resource-type "$ST_TYPE"
sleep 15
az storage account keys list --account-name "$ST" --resource-group "$RG_SHOP" --query "length(@)" --output tsv

Checkpoint: with the ReadOnly lock in place, show worked while keys list and tag update were refused. After removing the lock, keys list prints 2.

Task 6 · Move the account to the shared resource group

Other apps, such as the stores' tablets, will use the product photos too, so the account belongs in the shared group. Moving it changes its resource group, and therefore its ID, but not its region or its data.

OLD_ID="$ST_ID"
az resource move --destination-group "$RG_SHARED" --ids "$OLD_ID"

The move takes a minute or two. While it runs, both resource groups are locked against changes, but the storage account keeps serving data. When the prompt returns, compare the IDs:

ST_ID=$(az storage account show --name "$ST" --resource-group "$RG_SHARED" --query id --output tsv)
echo "old: $OLD_ID"
echo "new: $ST_ID"
az resource show --ids "$OLD_ID" --output none      # fails with ResourceNotFound: the old address is gone
az storage account show --name "$ST" --resource-group "$RG_SHARED" \
  --query "{group:resourceGroup, location:primaryLocation, tags:tags}" --output json

The location is unchanged and the account's own tags (app, env, owner) travelled with it, but it didn't pick up the shared group's costCenter=it: tags still don't inherit.

Tip: Prefer the portal? On the account's Overview page, select move next to Resource group, then Move to another resource group. The portal validates the move before it starts.

Checkpoint: the new ID contains rg-lunch04-shared-<suffix>, the old ID returns ResourceNotFound, and the account's location is still your LOCATION.

Task 7 · Find everything with Azure Resource Graph

Resource Graph searches every subscription you can read, in seconds. Its CLI commands live in the resource-graph extension; this setting lets the Azure CLI install extensions automatically, without asking:

az config set extension.use_dynamic_install=yes_without_prompt --only-show-errors

Resource groups live in the ResourceContainers table:

az graph query -q "ResourceContainers
  | where type =~ 'microsoft.resources/subscriptions/resourcegroups'
  | where tags.lunch == '04'
  | project name, location, project=tostring(tags.project), costCenter=tostring(tags.costCenter)" \
  --query "data[]" --output table

Resources live in the Resources table:

az graph query -q "Resources | where tags.app == 'product-images' | project name, type, resourceGroup, location" \
  --query "data[]" --output table

# Proof that tags don't inherit: no resource carries the shared group's costCenter=it
az graph query -q "Resources | where tags.costCenter == 'it' | project name, resourceGroup" \
  --query "data[]" --output table

Resource Graph is an index of your resources, so a change you made seconds ago may take a little while to appear. If a result looks stale, wait a minute and run the query again.

Tip: Prefer the portal? Search for Resource Graph Explorer, paste a query without the az graph query -q part and select Run query. You can save queries and pin results to a dashboard.

Checkpoint: the first query lists both resource groups with their project and cost centre, the second lists the storage account in the shared group, and the third returns no rows.

Task 8 (optional) · A management group in your own tenant

Warning: Do this only in your own tenant, for example the one created with your free account, where you are a Global Administrator. Management groups are tenant-wide: in a company tenant you could affect other people's governance, or your administrators may have blocked it. Never move a work subscription. The first management group in a tenant can take up to 15 minutes to appear, because Azure first sets up the root management group.

MG="mg-nusa-lab-${SUFFIX}"
az account management-group create --name "$MG" --display-name "Nusantara Retail (lab)" --output none
az account management-group show --name "$MG" \
  --query "{name:name, displayName:displayName, parent:details.parent.displayName}" --output table

The new group's parent is the Tenant root group. In the portal (Management groups) you can see your subscription under the Tenant root group, next to the new, empty management group. Leave the subscription where it is; Lunch 31 covers designing and filling a hierarchy. cleanup.sh deletes this management group for you.

Checkpoint: az account management-group show prints your group with Tenant Root Group as its parent. If you get an authorization error, your tenant requires permission to create management groups; skip this task.

Break it and fix it

Pak Budi decides to "protect" the whole shared resource group with a ReadOnly lock, without telling anyone:

az lock create --name lock-protect-shared --lock-type ReadOnly --resource-group "$RG_SHARED" \
  --notes "Added by Pak Budi" --output none
sleep 15

Now try a harmless change on the storage account:

az tag update --resource-id "$ST_ID" --operation Merge --tags reviewed=yes --output none

Symptom: the update fails with ScopeLocked, yet you never put a lock on the storage account. Find out where the lock lives and fix it.

Hint and fix

Locks are inherited. Listing the locks that apply to a resource includes the ones on its resource group and subscription, and each lock's ID shows the scope where it was set:

az lock list --resource-group "$RG_SHARED" --resource "$ST" --resource-type "$ST_TYPE" \
  --query "[].{name:name, level:level, scope:id}" --output table

The ID of lock-protect-shared ends at the resource group, not at the storage account. Remove it and retry:

az lock delete --name lock-protect-shared --resource-group "$RG_SHARED"
sleep 15
az tag update --resource-id "$ST_ID" --operation Merge --tags reviewed=yes --output none && echo "Fixed."

What should Pak Budi have used? A CanNotDelete lock protects the group from deletion without blocking everyday changes, and role assignments decide who may change things.

Troubleshooting

Symptom | Likely cause | Fix
(AuthorizationFailed) ... does not have authorization to perform action 'Microsoft.Authorization/locks/write' | You are Contributor, not Owner or User Access Administrator | Use a subscription where you are Owner, such as your own free account
(ScopeLocked) The scope '...' cannot perform delete operation because following scope(s) are locked | A lock on the resource or one of its parents | az lock list --resource-group ... --resource ... --resource-type ... shows every lock that applies; remove the right one
az resource move fails with ScopeLocked | A ReadOnly lock on the source or destination resource group (or the subscription) | Remove the lock, then move again
az resource show --ids "$OLD_ID" says ResourceNotFound | Expected after the move: the ID changed | Use the new ID from Task 6
az graph query asks to install an extension or says the command isn't found | The resource-graph extension isn't installed yet | Run the az config set extension.use_dynamic_install=yes_without_prompt line from Task 7, or az extension add --name resource-graph
A Resource Graph query doesn't show a change you just made | The index is still catching up | Wait a minute and run the query again
(StorageAccountAlreadyTaken) The storage account named ... is already taken. | Storage account names are global | Run bash cleanup.sh, then rm ~/.azlunches-suffix, source ../common/config.sh again and restart from Task 1
ensure_rg fails with ScopeLocked when you rerun Task 1 | A lock from Task 4, 5 or the break-and-fix exercise is still in place | Remove it (see the break-and-fix hint), then rerun
Management group creation fails with AuthorizationFailed | Hierarchy protection in your tenant requires permissions to create management groups | Skip Task 8; it is optional
